name: Neck harness lifts

lead: A neck harness holds a weight so the neck can be trained with progressive resistance, the way other muscles are.
Lifters use it to add neck thickness, which they associate with a stronger physique.

paras: Muscle growth from progressive loading of the neck flexors and extensors.
The cervical spine is involved, so form and gradual progression are commonly stressed.

chain: Weighted harness loads the neck extensors and flexors
Thicker neck and fuller upper-body frame
angle.text: Loading the neck progressively with a harness is intended to add muscle to the back and sides of the neck, which proponents say fills out the neck and frame, particularly visible in clothing. Training studies cited by coaches report increases in neck muscle size and strength.[5][6]

lead: Neck harness lifts are a form of neck training in which a head harness holds a weight plate or chain, and the lifter performs extension, flexion or side-bending against that load. The aim is to build the muscles of the neck, which thickens the neck and, in lifters' words, makes the upper body look more muscular and masculine; the harness is also a staple of combat-sport and contact-sport preparation [1][2].

In looksmaxxing and lifting communities, neck size is discussed as part of a stronger, more imposing frame, and neck work appears in training logs on forums such as T Nation alongside presses and pulls [3][4]. Strength coaches such as Bret Contreras and Jeff Nippard argue that heavy compound lifts alone may not add much neck size and that direct neck work is the way to target it [5][1].

Research on neck training spans small training studies measuring neck strength and muscle size, and sports-medicine work on whether stronger necks relate to lower concussion rates. The research is mostly not specific to harnesses, and no published study found tests how a thicker neck is perceived [5][6][7].
infobox: Head harness with plate or chain; also bands, towels, manual resistance, neck machines[2][5]
Neck extensors and flexors, lateral neck muscles, upper trapezius[1]
About 13% neck muscle cross-sectional area over 12 weeks in one study cited by coaches[5][1]
Gradual progression and controlled range; professional advice with prior neck injury[2]

paras: The lifter wears a harness on the head with a weight hanging from it, or attaches a band or cable, and moves the neck through controlled ranges, commonly extension, flexion and lateral flexion. Coaches describe a harness as the main tool needed for basic neck work, with bands for lateral movement and partner or banded resistance for other directions [2]. Training logs on lifting forums show neck work mixed into programmes alongside heavy compound lifts [3][8].

Neck strength differs by direction: Contreras writes that extension is strongest, followed by lateral bending, flexion and rotation, and recommends training all six directions with methods ranging from isometric holds to harness work [5].

Neck bridges and manual-resistance drills are long-standing parts of wrestling and grappling practice, and the elitefts author, a Brazilian jiu-jitsu black belt, describes starting practice with neck bridges [2]. Weighted head harnesses and neck machines are the gym-based extensions of that work. The elitefts article lists a basic head and neck harness, a padded harness and the Iron Neck, a portable 360-degree resistance system [2].

Strength athletes also use neck work: powerlifters rely on neck retraction under the squat bar, and the elitefts article advises finishing lifts with neck training instead of fatiguing the neck first [2].

Community discussion links a thicker neck with a more imposing appearance and treats the harness as the standard tool for progressive loading. Nippard argues that bigger neck and trap muscles make a person look more muscular and masculine, especially in clothing [1]. Forum lifters also mention related upper-back work such as pulldowns for posture and shoulder position [9].

Trainers describe harness extensions for the back of the neck and plate-loaded or manual-resistance curls for the front and sides, and discuss frequency of about two sessions per week; Contreras notes that two sessions per week outperformed one in a study he cites [1][5].

sections.h: What studies on neck size report
paras: Contreras summarises a 1997 study by Conley and colleagues in which adding neck-specific work to a resistance programme increased neck extension strength by 34%, while resistance training alone did not, and cites about a 13% increase in neck muscle cross-sectional area over three months with combined training [5]. Nippard describes the same 12-week result, in which adding direct neck extension work produced a 13% increase in neck cross-sectional area and the group without it saw none [1].

Contreras also lists studies in which 8 weeks of training raised isometric neck strength by about 38 to 40%, in which football players with targeted neck training outperformed those without it, and in which machine training outperformed band training over 10 weeks [5]. Nippard notes that neck-training research is limited and mentions a Navy recruit study with 10 participants whose 1.4 cm circumference gain was not statistically significant [1].

A 2019 clinical review in the Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy describes how neck strength, girth, strength imbalance and head posture relate to sports-related concussion risk. It reports that one prospective study, by Collins and colleagues, found each one-pound increase in neck strength was associated with 5% lower concussion risk, significant in male but not female high school athletes, and that stronger necks are associated with lower head acceleration in laboratory studies [6]. The review states no age- or sex-specific strength values linked to reduced risk have been established [6].

A 2018 protocol paper describes the TRAIN study, which planned a three-year neck-strengthening programme in student-athletes at six Minnesota schools with strength measured every six months; it reports hypotheses rather than results [7]. Coaches describe neck work for contact-sport athletes as a safety measure rather than a performance booster [2].

The neck contains the cervical spine, and coaching sources advise starting conservatively, progressing slowly, keeping movements controlled, avoiding painful ranges and consulting a qualified professional with a history of neck injury, concussion, neurological symptoms or cervical problems [2]. Contreras calls the neck delicate and describes isometric training as probably the safest route, noting that discs face more stress at end ranges under load; reader comments on his article mention headaches, soreness and nerve tingling [5].
Nippard suggests moderate rep ranges taken close to failure with control, noting that heavy loading may strain connective tissue, and that neck soreness can be significant [1].

No studies found that test head-harness lifts on perceived appearance. Related research includes the training studies on neck strength and size summarised by coaches [5][1], a clinical review of neck strength and concussion risk [6], and the TRAIN trial protocol [7].

lore.intro: Neck training appears in lifting logs and physique discussions as an accessory habit, and coaches who write about it present it both as a size builder and as protective work for athletes [3][4][1][2].

claims.claim: A bigger neck makes the frame look stronger and more masculine.
Heavy compound lifts alone do not grow the neck, so direct work is needed.
Direct neck training measurably increases neck muscle size.
A stronger neck lowers concussion risk.
Neck work carries injury risk if loaded heavily or done poorly.
Training the neck twice a week beats once a week.

timeline.event: Pollock and colleagues report that one set was enough for neck strength gains and twice-weekly training beat once-weekly, per Contreras. [5]
Maeda and colleagues report about 38 to 40% isometric neck strength gains after 8 weeks of training, per Contreras. [5]
Conley and colleagues find that adding neck extension work to resistance training increased neck extension strength and muscle size, while lifting alone did not, per Contreras. [5]
Ylinen and colleagues report on a year-long strength-training study in 180 women with chronic neck pain, per Contreras. [5]
Burnett and colleagues compare machine and band neck training over 10 weeks, per Contreras. [5]

Collins and colleagues link weaker neck strength with higher concussion susceptibility in high school contact sports; Eckner and colleagues link stronger necks with smaller head response to impulsive loads. [7][6]
TRAIN study protocol published for a three-year neck-strengthening programme in student-athletes. [7]
JOSPT clinical review summarises the cervical spine's role in sports-related concussion and calls for prospective studies. [6]
